The challenge: detecting errors without reading the encoded state

Quantum information is vulnerable to bit-flip and phase-flip errors. For QUBLITZ 2026, this project implemented four challenge levels, including recovery circuits for Levels 1–3 and a Level-4 syndrome classifier that distinguishes I, X, Y, and Z errors using two measured bits.

Circuit optimization and verification

The project used exact-state simulation, native-gate compilation, and calibration-aware placement to reduce circuit overhead while preserving the intended syndrome extraction. In the representative +i/Y1 execution circuit, CZ gates fell from 24 to 11 and circuit depth from 45 to 17.

  • 78 of 78 ideal exact-native Level-4 cases passed for each variant.
  • The archived regression suite reports 803 passing tests.

Results on real quantum hardware

A recorded IQM Garnet experiment compared eight balanced circuits with 256 shots each. The original design classified 759 of 1,024 shots correctly (74.12%); the improved design classified 921 of 1,024 (89.94%). The observed gain was 15.82 percentage points, with all shots retained.

The saved execution receipt, native circuit definition, measurement counts, and calibration identifiers were cross-checked locally. The repository preserves the execution artifacts and analysis workflow for reproducibility.

What the results do and do not establish

The hardware metric is syndrome-classification success, not logical-state fidelity. Hardware recovery for Levels 1–3 was not measured; the comparison also does not isolate the individual causes of the improvement or establish globally optimal compilation. The recorded hardware evidence is reproduced from saved artifacts rather than a new server retrieval.
